text: Any fortress can be taken if a donkey laden with gold can climb up to it.
variants: No fortress is impregnable if a donkey laden with gold can reach it.
documented_in: Cicero, Letters to Atticus 1.16.12; Plutarch, Moralia, Sayings of Kings and Commanders (Philip). English wording varies by translation.
lens: Ask what the walls are made of: most defenses fail through the people who hold the gate, not the stone. If you are defending, look for who can be bought; if you are attacking, look for the price instead of the siege.
impact_rationale: Ancient, repeatedly borne out (bribery, insider threats, social engineering), and it reframes 'strong vs weak' as 'who has incentives'.

text: Come and take them.
variants: Molon labe (Μολὼν λαβέ)
Come and get them.
documented_in: Plutarch, Moralia, Sayings of Spartans (Leonidas son of Anaxandridas): his reply when Xerxes wrote demanding that the Greeks hand over their arms.
lens: A demand to give up your means of resistance before the fight is the real battle. Refusing it puts the cost of enforcement back on the stronger side.
impact_rationale: Enduring emblem of refusing to disarm under threat; a clear lens on ultimatums, though it can shade into bravado.
counter_sayings: The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.

text: If.
attribution: The Spartans (reply to Philip II of Macedon)
documented_in: Plutarch, Moralia, On Talkativeness (De garrulitate): Philip wrote 'If I invade Laconia, I will drive you out'; the Spartans replied 'If.' The source of the word 'laconic'.
lens: A threat built on a condition is only as strong as the condition. Answer the 'if', not the bluster, and say less than they expect.
impact_rationale: The canonical laconic reply; shows how brevity and calm deflate a threat. Narrower use than the top entries.

text: If we are victorious in one more battle with the Romans, we shall be utterly ruined.
variants: One more such victory and we are lost.
documented_in: Plutarch, Life of Pyrrhus 21, after the battle of Asculum (279 BC). Origin of the phrase 'Pyrrhic victory'.
lens: Count what the win costs, not just whether you win. A victory that spends what you need for the next fight is a slow defeat.
impact_rationale: Gave the language a term; applies to lawsuits, price wars, and office politics alike.

text: Bad is the plan that cannot be changed.
variants: Malum est consilium quod mutari non potest.
It is a bad plan that admits of no modification.
documented_in: Publilius Syrus, Sententiae (1st century BC), under M: 'Malum est consilium quod mutari non potest.'
lens: Before committing, ask what would make you change course and whether you still could. Rigidity is a cost to price in, not a virtue.
impact_rationale: Two thousand years old and still the core of contingency planning; pairs usefully with commitment sayings.

text: If one does not know to which port one is sailing, no wind is favorable.
variants: Ignoranti quem portum petat nullus suus ventus est.
documented_in: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales) 71.3.
lens: When every option looks equally good or bad, the problem may be the goal, not the options. Settle the destination before judging the winds.
impact_rationale: Turns a confusing choice into a question about purpose; endures in management and personal decision-making.

text: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
variants: There are more things that frighten us than crush us.
Plura sunt quae nos terrent quam quae premunt, et saepius opinione quam re laboramus.
documented_in: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales) 13.4.
lens: Separate what is happening from what you fear will happen. Most of the weight you feel may be forecast, not fact.
impact_rationale: Stoic insight later echoed by cognitive therapy; changes how you weigh a frightening situation.
counter_sayings: An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

text: We all have strength enough to endure the misfortunes of others.
variants: Nous avons tous assez de force pour supporter les maux d'autrui.
documented_in: La Rochefoucauld, Maximes (1665), maxim 19.
lens: Advice and sympathy are cheap when the cost falls on someone else. Discount counsel from people who will not bear the consequences, including yourself when judging others.
impact_rationale: Sharp and durable observation of human nature; useful when weighing other people's advice.

text: Three may keep a secret, if two of them are dead.
documented_in: Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1735). Franklin often reworked older proverbs; the line is his published wording.
lens: Every person you tell is a possible leak. If the secret matters, shrink the circle, or assume it will get out and plan for that.
impact_rationale: Memorable and practically true; a simple check on information security and confidences.

text: An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
documented_in: English proverb. Used by Benjamin Franklin in a letter on fire prevention in the Pennsylvania Gazette, 4 February 1735 ('an Ounce of Prevention is worth a Pound of Cure').
lens: Compare the small cost of acting now with the large cost of fixing it later. Problems that are cheap today are often the ones being ignored.
impact_rationale: Widely proven in medicine, engineering and maintenance; directly changes what you prioritize.

text: Look before you leap.
variants: Look ere ye leap.
documented_in: English proverb; in John Heywood, A Dialogue Conteinyng the Nomber in Effect of All the Prouerbes in the Englishe Tongue (1546): 'look ere ye leap'.
lens: Before an irreversible move, take one more look at where you will land. The question is whether the leap can be undone.
impact_rationale: Universal and true, but so familiar it rarely changes anyone's view; most useful when paired with its counter.

text: He who hesitates is lost.
variants: The woman that deliberates is lost.
documented_in: Proverb derived from Joseph Addison, Cato: A Tragedy (1713), Act IV: 'The woman that deliberates is lost.'
lens: Waiting is also a decision, with its own costs. Ask what the delay is buying you, and whether the window is closing.
impact_rationale: Familiar, but a needed corrective to over-caution; most powerful in tension with 'look before you leap'.

text: It ain't what you don't know that gets you into trouble. It's what you know for sure that just ain't so.
documented_in: Widely quoted as Mark Twain, e.g. the opening epigraph of the film The Big Short (2015). No source in Twain's writings; Quote Investigator (2018) traces similar sayings to the humorist Josh Billings in the 1870s and later variants to others.
lens: The dangerous gaps are not the questions you know you have, but the beliefs you never question. List what you are certain of and test the one that would hurt most if wrong.
impact_rationale: Strong lens on overconfidence and hidden assumptions; kept despite false attribution per the no-fabrication rule.

text: All warfare is based on deception.
documented_in: The Art of War, ch. 1 'Laying Plans' (Lionel Giles translation, 1910). The text's single authorship is traditional, not established.
lens: In an adversarial situation, assume what you are shown is chosen for you to see. Ask what the other side wants you to believe, and why.
impact_rationale: Foundational in strategic thought; reframes competitive signals as possibly staged.

text: If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.
documented_in: The Art of War, ch. 3 'Attack by Stratagem' (Lionel Giles translation, 1910). Single authorship traditional.
lens: Most losses come from misjudging one side of the comparison. Before acting, check both: what they can really do, and what you can really do.
impact_rationale: Durable framework for any contest; points at the two most common blind spots.

text: Trust in God, but tie your camel.
variants: Tie it, and rely upon God.
documented_in: Jami' at-Tirmidhi (hadith collection): a man asked whether to tie his camel and trust God, or leave it untied and trust God; the reply was 'Tie it and rely upon God.' Widespread as an Arabic and Persian proverb.
lens: Faith, hope, or optimism does not replace doing the basic precautions. Do your part, then let go of what you cannot control.
impact_rationale: Cross-cultural and balances action with acceptance; a useful corrective to both fatalism and anxiety.

text: This too shall pass.
variants: And this, too, shall pass away.
documented_in: From Persian Sufi tradition (the story of a king's ring). Retold by Abraham Lincoln, address to the Wisconsin State Agricultural Society, Milwaukee, 30 September 1859: 'And this, too, shall pass away.'
lens: Whatever state you are in, good or bad, is temporary. In bad times it gives endurance; in good times it is a warning against assuming the run will last.
impact_rationale: Works in both directions, which is rare; endured across Persian, Jewish and English traditions.

text: No plan of operations extends with any certainty beyond the first contact with the main hostile force.
variants: No plan survives contact with the enemy.
documented_in: Moltke, 'Über Strategie' (On Strategy), 1871. The short form 'No plan survives contact with the enemy' is a later paraphrase.
lens: Expect the plan to break on first contact with reality, and invest in people's ability to adapt rather than in the plan's detail.
impact_rationale: Military and business experience confirm it constantly; shifts effort from planning to adaptability.

text: Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.
documented_in: Eisenhower, remarks at the National Defense Executive Reserve Conference, Washington, 14 November 1957 (Public Papers of the Presidents). He said he had heard it long before in the Army.
lens: The value of planning is the understanding it builds, not the document. When the plan breaks, that understanding is what lets you replan fast.
impact_rationale: Resolves the apparent paradox of planning under uncertainty; complements Moltke.

text: Make haste slowly.
variants: Festina lente
σπεῦδε βραδέως (speude bradeos)
documented_in: Suetonius, Life of Augustus 25.4 (a favorite saying of Augustus, in Greek); Erasmus, Adagia II.i.1 'Festina lente'.
lens: Speed and care are not opposites. Move steadily on the parts that can't be redone, and quickly on the rest.
impact_rationale: Long-lived (Augustus, Erasmus, the Aldine press emblem) and dissolves a false choice between haste and caution.

text: In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.
variants: In regione caecorum rex est luscus.
documented_in: Proverb collected by Erasmus, Adagia ('In regione caecorum rex est luscus').
lens: Advantage is relative to the field. You may not need to be excellent, only better than the alternatives, and the reverse holds when the field improves.
impact_rationale: Durable insight about relative advantage in markets and careers.

text: The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
attribution: The Athenian envoys at Melos (as written by Thucydides)
documented_in: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 5.89 (the Melian Dialogue). Speeches in Thucydides are his reconstructions. Wording varies by translation.
lens: Appeals to fairness do not move a party that has no need to be fair. Look at the real balance of power and what each side can actually do.
impact_rationale: Cornerstone of realist thought for 2,400 years; a hard, clarifying lens on negotiations with unequal power.

text: Stand a little out of my sun.
variants: Stand out of my light.
documented_in: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.38; Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14. His reply when Alexander offered him anything he wished.
lens: When someone powerful offers you anything, it is worth noticing that you may not need what they have. Wanting little is a form of freedom in a negotiation.
impact_rationale: Famous anecdote that reframes power as dependent on what the other person wants.

text: The die is cast.
variants: Alea iacta est
documented_in: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar 32, at the crossing of the Rubicon (49 BC). Plutarch (Caesar 32; Pompey 60) says he spoke it in Greek.
lens: Some decisions remove the option to go back, and that can be the point. Once committed, put your energy into succeeding, not re-arguing the choice.
impact_rationale: Defines the irreversible decision; useful both as a warning before and a discipline after committing.
